clinicalPearls: The Bartholin glands lie at the posterior aspect of the vaginal introitus and secrete mucus for lubrication; obstruction of their duct leads to cyst formation and secondary infection produces an abscess
An abscess typically presents as a painful, tender, fluctuant swelling in the posterolateral labium majus that can make sitting and walking difficult
Infection is usually polymicrobial with vaginal and enteric flora, though sexually transmitted organisms such as gonorrhoea and chlamydia should be considered
Definitive treatment relies on drainage rather than antibiotics alone, and simple incision and drainage alone has a high recurrence rate
Placement of a Word catheter or marsupialisation creates an epithelialised tract that allows continued drainage and reduces recurrence
Antibiotics are reserved for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, immunocompromise, or high-risk sexually transmitted infection rather than routine drained abscesses
In women over the age of forty, and particularly postmenopausal women, a persistent or atypical Bartholin mass should raise concern for the rare Bartholin gland carcinoma and prompt biopsy
Sitz baths and analgesia support symptom relief and can encourage spontaneous drainage of small abscesses
reference.pathophysiology: Obstruction of the Bartholin duct, often following inflammation or inspissated secretions, causes retention of mucus and cystic dilatation of the gland. Stasis within the obstructed duct favours bacterial proliferation, and secondary infection with mixed vaginal, enteric, and occasionally sexually transmitted organisms produces a walled-off collection of pus. The resulting abscess generates local inflammation, oedema, and pain, and if untreated may point and rupture spontaneously or recur once the duct re-obstructs.
additionalDifferentials: Vulvar epidermal inclusion or sebaceous cyst
Vulvar abscess from other skin flora or hidradenitis suppurativa
Bartholin gland carcinoma in older women
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination to confirm location, fluctuance, and surrounding cellulitis
Swab of abscess fluid at drainage for culture and sensitivity
Testing for gonorrhoea and chlamydia including nucleic acid amplification where appropriate
Biopsy of the gland wall in women over forty or with atypical or recurrent masses
Consideration of glucose testing to identify undiagnosed diabetes in recurrent infection
redFlags: Spreading vulval cellulitis, systemic sepsis, or features suggesting necrotising infection
Rapidly enlarging or irregular mass, or one in a postmenopausal woman, raising suspicion of carcinoma
Recurrent abscesses that may indicate underlying diabetes or immunosuppression
Severe pain with induration extending beyond the gland
Failure to resolve after adequate drainage
reference.prognosis: Most Bartholin abscesses resolve well after adequate drainage, and techniques that create a lasting drainage tract, such as catheter placement or marsupialisation, substantially lower recurrence. Recurrent disease may require repeat procedures or gland excision, and the outlook is excellent overall provided malignancy is excluded in older or atypical cases.
pitfalls: Treating with antibiotics alone without adequate drainage
Relying on simple incision and drainage, which frequently recurs, instead of a definitive drainage procedure
Failing to test for sexually transmitted infections when relevant
Overlooking Bartholin carcinoma in an older woman with a persistent solid mass
Not investigating recurrent abscesses for underlying diabetes
management: Incision and drainage with insertion of a Word catheter to create an epithelialised drainage tract
Marsupialisation for large or recurrent abscesses to reduce recurrence
Antibiotics reserved for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, immunocompromise or high-risk sexually transmitted infection, covering polymicrobial vaginal and enteric flora
Testing and treatment for gonorrhoea and chlamydia where indicated, with partner notification
Sitz baths and analgesia for symptomatic relief
Gland excision for recurrent disease resistant to drainage procedures
Biopsy of the gland in women over forty or with atypical lesions to exclude carcinoma
